entries.meaning: Facts and figures collected for reference or analysis.
examples: The data is stored on three separate servers.
All the data was lost in the crash.
We need more data before deciding.
The data are consistent with the hypothesis.
These data were collected over six years.
Each datum is timestamped at collection.
Elevations are measured from a fixed datum.

senses.head: Information collected for analysis
body: Usually treated as a mass noun. (данные)
examples: The data is stored on three separate servers.
All the data was lost in the crash.
We need more data before deciding.

senses.head: In scientific writing — a plural
examples: The data are consistent with the hypothesis.
These data were collected over six years.

senses.head: A single fact — datum
examples: Each datum is timestamped at collection.
Elevations are measured from a fixed datum.

entries.countability: data is countable in science, uncountable in general use
entries.agreement: either — the data are (science) / the data is (general)
entries.variants: both /ˈdeɪtə/ and /ˈdætə/ are standard in American English
entries.contrast: The singular datum is now rare outside surveying and statistics; almost nobody says one datum. For the plural, both verbs are defensible: journals still require the data are, while everyday and business English overwhelmingly says the data is. Neither is an error, but know your audience.

entries.meaning: A means of communication or expression; a substance something exists in; also a person who claims to contact spirits.
examples: Television is still a powerful medium.
The media has moved on to the next story.
Social media changed how the campaign was run.
Oil is her preferred medium.
He works across several media.
The bacteria were grown in a nutrient medium.
Sound needs a medium to travel through.
Two mediums were hired for the show.
I'll take the medium in blue.

senses.head: A channel of communication
body: Plural media, often treated as a singular mass noun. (средства массовой информации)
examples: Television is still a powerful medium.
The media has moved on to the next story.
Social media changed how the campaign was run.

senses.head: A material an artist works in
examples: Oil is her preferred medium.
He works across several media.

senses.head: A substance in which something grows or travels
examples: The bacteria were grown in a nutrient medium.
Sound needs a medium to travel through.

senses.head: A person claiming to contact the dead
examples: Two mediums were hired for the show.

senses.head: A middle size or degree
examples: I'll take the medium in blue.

entries.agreement: either — the media is (the press as one body) / are (the outlets)
entries.variants: media (communication, art materials, biology) · mediums (spiritualists, clothing sizes)
entries.contrast: The plural depends entirely on the sense. Channels of communication and artistic materials take media; people who claim to contact the dead, and shirt sizes, take mediums. When media means the press, American English treats it as singular: the media is covering it closely.

entries.meaning: A single-celled microorganism.
examples: This bacterium survives in boiling water.
Bacteria are responsible for the smell.
Most bacteria in the gut are harmless.
A single bacterium can divide every twenty minutes.
The sample contained three species of bacteria.

senses.head: The organism
examples: This bacterium survives in boiling water.
Bacteria are responsible for the smell.
Most bacteria in the gut are harmless.
A single bacterium can divide every twenty minutes.
The sample contained three species of bacteria.

entries.agreement: plural verb in careful use — bacteria are present
entries.contrast: ✗ A bacteria for one organism is extremely common in speech and still considered an error in writing — the singular is bacterium. Note that bacteria keeps its plural verb far more reliably than data does, because the singular is still in active use.

entries.meaning: The subjects taught by a school or in a program.
examples: The curriculum changes every four years.
Both curricula emphasize writing.
Music was cut from the curriculum.
State curriculums vary widely.
She helped design the new science curriculum.

senses.head: A course of study
examples: The curriculum changes every four years.
Both curricula emphasize writing.
Music was cut from the curriculum.
State curriculums vary widely.
She helped design the new science curriculum.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the curricula were revised
entries.variants: curricula is commoner in education writing; curriculums is accepted
entries.contrast: Note the Latin phrase curriculum vitae — a résumé — whose plural is curricula vitae. Americans usually just say CV or résumé.

entries.meaning: A written record or communication, especially within an organization.
examples: The memorandum was circulated to all partners.
Internal memoranda were subpoenaed.
Both sides signed a memorandum of understanding.
She filed the memorandums by date.
A confidential memorandum leaked to the press.

senses.head: An official note
examples: The memorandum was circulated to all partners.
Internal memoranda were subpoenaed.
Both sides signed a memorandum of understanding.
She filed the memorandums by date.
A confidential memorandum leaked to the press.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the memoranda were filed
entries.variants: both plurals are correct; the shortened memo / memos is far commoner in speech
entries.contrast: In everyday American offices nobody says memorandum — they say memo. The full form survives in law and diplomacy, as in memorandum of understanding.

entries.meaning: A direct popular vote on a single question.
examples: The referendum passed by four points.
Two referendums are on the November ballot.
Voters rejected the referendum.

The election became a referendum on the mayor.

senses.head: A public vote
examples: The referendum passed by four points.
Two referendums are on the November ballot.
Voters rejected the referendum.
Several referenda were held that decade.

senses.head: Figuratively — a test of public opinion
examples: The election became a referendum on the mayor.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both referendums failed
entries.variants: referendums is preferred in American English and in most style guides
entries.contrast: Grammarians argue that referenda is technically wrong because the Latin word is a gerund, not a neuter noun. In practice both appear; referendums is safer.

entries.meaning: A period of a thousand years.
examples: The site has been occupied for two millennia.
A new millennium began in 2001.
These traditions go back millennia.
The stone has stood here for three millennia.
Historians divide the millennium into four periods.

senses.head: A thousand-year period
examples: The site has been occupied for two millennia.
A new millennium began in 2001.
These traditions go back millennia.
The stone has stood here for three millennia.
Historians divide the millennium into four periods.

entries.agreement: plural verb — three millennia have passed
entries.variants: millennia is much commoner
entries.contrast: Two l's and two n's — the commonest misspelling in the word is ✗ millenium. It comes from mille 'thousand' and annus 'year'.

entries.meaning: A layer, especially of rock or of society.
examples: Each stratum represents thousands of years.
The strata are tilted almost vertically.
Fossils appear in the lower strata.
The policy affects every stratum of society.
All social strata were represented in the survey.

senses.head: A layer of rock or soil
examples: Each stratum represents thousands of years.

Fossils appear in the lower strata.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the strata are clearly visible
entries.variants: ✗ stratums is rare and best avoided
entries.contrast: ✗ A strata for one layer is a common error — the singular is stratum. The related stratosphere comes from the same root.

entries.meaning: An error in printing or writing, listed as a correction.
examples: A single erratum was noted in the second printing.
The errata are listed on the last page.
The publisher issued an errata sheet.
Twelve errata were found after publication.
Each erratum gives the page and the corrected text.

senses.head: A published correction
examples: A single erratum was noted in the second printing.
The errata are listed on the last page.
The publisher issued an errata sheet.
Twelve errata were found after publication.
Each erratum gives the page and the corrected text.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the errata are listed at the back
entries.variants: ✗ erratums is not used
entries.contrast: In practice the word appears almost only in the plural, and often as the fixed phrase errata sheet — the slip of corrections tucked into a printed book.

entries.meaning: Something added, especially to a document or book.
examples: The contract includes a two-page addendum.
Both addenda were signed separately.
An addendum clarifies the delivery terms.
Several addendums were added over the years.
The addenda appear after the index.

senses.head: An added section or clause
examples: The contract includes a two-page addendum.
Both addenda were signed separately.
An addendum clarifies the delivery terms.
Several addendums were added over the years.
The addenda appear after the index.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the addenda were attached
entries.variants: addenda is commoner in formal and legal writing

entries.meaning: An academic conference or meeting on a particular subject.
examples: She presented at a symposium in Chicago.
Two symposia are scheduled for the fall.
The symposium runs for three days.
Papers from both symposiums will be published.
A symposium on climate policy opens Monday.

senses.head: A scholarly meeting
examples: She presented at a symposium in Chicago.
Two symposia are scheduled for the fall.
The symposium runs for three days.
Papers from both symposiums will be published.
A symposium on climate policy opens Monday.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both symposia were canceled
entries.variants: both plurals are standard in American academic use
entries.contrast: From Greek by way of Latin, originally a drinking party — literally 'drinking together'.

entries.meaning: A place or occasion for public discussion; also an online discussion board.
examples: The town hall is a forum for local complaints.
Several public forums were held before the vote.
This is not the right forum for that argument.

senses.head: A place for public discussion
examples: The town hall is a forum for local complaints.
Several public forums were held before the vote.
This is not the right forum for that argument.

senses.head: An online discussion board
examples: He posts on three different forums.
The forums are moderated by volunteers.

senses.head: The public square of a Roman town
examples: The imperial fora lie north of the Colosseum.

entries.plural: forums — usual · fora in classical contexts
entries.agreement: plural verb — the forums are moderated
entries.variants: forums everywhere in modern English; fora only of Roman marketplaces
entries.contrast: Although Latin, this word takes a regular English plural in every ordinary use. Fora sounds precious outside archaeology. The same is true of album → albums, stadium → stadiums, museum → museums, and asylum → asylums.

entries.meaning: A large enclosed sports ground with seating.
examples: The stadium holds seventy thousand people.
Both stadiums were built for the same tournament.
They're tearing down the old stadium.
Four new stadiums opened that year.
The stadium was half empty by the fourth quarter.

senses.head: The building
examples: The stadium holds seventy thousand people.
Both stadiums were built for the same tournament.
They're tearing down the old stadium.
Four new stadiums opened that year.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both stadiums were sold out
entries.variants: stadiums is standard American English; stadia is chiefly British and technical
entries.contrast: ✗ Stadia sounds odd to American ears in ordinary use, though it appears in architecture writing. Use stadiums.

entries.meaning: A building where objects of interest are displayed.
examples: The museum opens at ten.
All the city museums are free on the first Sunday.
She works at a natural history museum.
Both museums closed for renovation.
The painting moved to a private museum.

senses.head: The institution
examples: The museum opens at ten.
All the city museums are free on the first Sunday.
She works at a natural history museum.
Both museums closed for renovation.
The painting moved to a private museum.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the museums are free on Sundays
entries.contrast: ✗ Musea is never used. Note the stress: myoo-ZEE-uhm, on the second syllable, not ✗ MYOO-zee-uhm.

entries.meaning: A list of items to be discussed; also an underlying purpose.
examples: The agenda is short today.
Both agendas were circulated in advance.
That item is not on the agenda.
He clearly has his own agenda.
Competing agendas stalled the whole process.

senses.head: A list of items
examples: The agenda is short today.
Both agendas were circulated in advance.
That item is not on the agenda.

senses.head: An underlying purpose
examples: He clearly has his own agenda.
Competing agendas stalled the whole process.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the agenda is short
entries.pattern: a Latin plural that became an English singular
entries.variants: the Latin singular agendum has vanished from ordinary English
entries.contrast: This is the pattern completed. Agenda was the Latin plural of agendum; English reinterpreted it as a singular and built the regular plural agendas on top. Nobody now says ✗ the agenda are. Data and media are partway along the same road.

entries.meaning: A band of wavelengths; also a range of positions or conditions.
